The cougar once ranged throughout continental United States (with the exception of Alaska) and southern Canada. Today it has been extirpated from much of its former range, and two subspecies, the <u>eastern cougar</u> and <u>Florida panther</u>, are considered endangered. Collectively, these two subspecies were probably characteristic of the temperate deciduous forest biome, but never dominant members of their associations.
The <u>California bighorn</u> was once found from the Chilcotin River, British Columbia, south through the Cascades and other mountains of Washington and Oregon and Sierra Nevada to the vicinity of Mount Whitney western Nevada south probably to Mineral County. Here it was a characteristic member of the associations of the desert biome.
Although the <u>red-cockaded woodpecker</u> and <u>ivory-billed woodpecker</u>, were at one time widely distributed from southeastern Missouri to Virginia and North Carolina and southward, their specific requirements were too narrow for them to be considered characteristic members of the temperate deciduous forest biome. Habitat of the red-cockaded woodpecker is dependent upon availability of living pire trees diseased with redheart—essential for nest sites. Prior to the advent of modern timber management, however, over-aged pines were probably not so limiting to the distribution of the species throughout the southeastern pine forest associations. Similarly, the ivorybill was dependent for its distribution and well being upon the rather continuous stands of mature bottomland hardwoods found through southeastern United States. Fate of this woodpecker was undoubtedly sealed in the early days with settlement of the southeast and the nation's growing hunger for hardwood lumber.
